title: Iran fires back, insists on probe into B.C. shooting: Demand mirrors Kazemi request: [National Edition]
article: The federal government held its fire yesterday after Iran launched a new volley in the diplomatic row over the death and burial of a Montreal photojournalist, accusing police in British Columbia of the "criminal" killing of an Iranian.
"We're not going to enter into a war of words here," Foreign Affairs spokesman Reynald Doiron said. "Based on what we know, we don't think the situations can compare."

Iran's charges stemmed from a July 14 incident in Port Moody, B.C., during which Iranian Keyvan Tabesh, 18, was shot and killed by a police officer after he allegedly lunged at the plainclothes officer with a machete.

Tehran insisted on a rapid, transparent inquiry with wording that mirrored the Canadian government's demands for an investigation into the death in custody of Zahra Kazemi, 54, and the prosecution of those responsible.

Tehran's new offensive began less than 24 hours after Prime Minister Jean Chretien announced he was recalling Canada's ambassador to Iran to protest Ms. Kazemi's killing and her burial on Wednesday in Iran, contrary to the wishes of her son, Stephan Hachemi, and the Canadian government.
The government is mulling further penalties against Iran, including economic sanctions and curbs on government-to-government contacts and travel.

Mr. Hachemi, who lives in Montreal, and the Canadian government had demanded the body be returned to Canada for autopsy and burial. The government now is exploring legal and religious options for having the body exhumed and brought to Canada.
Iran dismissed as unjustified Canada's decision to recall ambassador Philip MacKinnon and began publicizing its complaints about the killing of Mr. Tabesh.

"Why have the Canadian police, who should safeguard the security of the people, committed this disgraceful crime which scared Iranian citizens living in Canada," Iranian state media quoted Foreign Ministry spokesman Hamid Reza Asefi as saying.
"Iran wants the Canadian government to give an explicit and transparent and satisfactory explanation about this criminal act and to hand over those responsible for this regrettable event to justice."

"There is no moral or legal equivalence between a man threatening police with a machete, as happened apparently in this incident in Canada, and a woman taking a picture of a building," said Canadian Alliance foreign affairs critic Stockwell Day.

"There is no moral equivalence at all to police officers in Canada fulfilling their duties, and always being subject to full investigation and reporting, with that and a regime like Iran's which consistently tortures and murders its own citizens and now the citizens of other countries."
Liberal MP Joe Peschisolido dismissed accusations the Iranian community in Canada was intimidated by the B.C. incident.

"They're worried about 18-year-old kids with machetes regardless of their nationalities, just like everybody else," said the MP for Richmond, B.C. "For the Iranian government to try to cover up their heinous acts by equating a very sad and tragic situation that occurred here in Vancouver to the brutal systematic beating of a photographer is just outrageous."

Bill Graham, the Foreign Affairs Minister, was unavailable for comment, but officials said he still wants to talk with his Iranian counterpart Kamal Kharazi, who is travelling.The government's silence is no accident. One official said it is loath to get sucked into a "spitting match" with Iran through the media.
Mr. MacKinnon returns to Canada today and is scheduled to make his first report to Foreign Affairs officials tomorrow.
